Warfarin is an oral anticoagulant. The mechanism of action is to bind to and inhibit the
enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase. This enzyme is coded by the gene, VKORC1. A
common polymorphism in VKORC1 (1639G>A) results in increased sensitivity to
warfarin (increased inhibition at a given warfarin concentration). Patients with one or two
alleles require progressively lower warfarin doses. (Less common variants are associated
with warfarin resistance.) The risk of over-anticoagulation is hemorrhage, including into
the brain.

weight, the daily dose of warfarin for therapeutic anticoagulation varies 20 times in the
population, ranging from 0.5 mg/day to 10 mg/day (3.5 to 70 mg/week). Polymorphisms
of VKORC1 accounts for the majority of variation, but CYP2C9 polymorphism also
contributes.

Clinical example:
The degree of inhibition produced by a competitive antagonist depends on the concentration
Of antagonist. The competitive B-adrenoceptor antagonist propranolo/provides a useful
example. Patients receiving a fixed dose of this drug exhibit a wide range of plasma
concentrations, owing to differences among individuals in clearance of propranolol. As a
result, inhibitory effects on physiologic responses to norepinephrine and epinephrine
(endogenous adrenergic receptor agonists) may vary widely, and the dose of propranolol
must be adjusted accordingly.
Clinical response to a competitive antagonist also depends on the concentration of agonist
that is competing for binding to receptors. Again, propranolol provides a useful example:
When this drug is administered at moderate doses sufficient to block the effect of basal levels
of the neurotransmitter norepinephrine, resting heart rate is decreased. However, the
increase in the release of norepinephrine and epinephrine that occurs with exercise, postural
changes, or emotional stress may suffice to overcome this competitive antagonism.
Accordingly, the same dose of propranolol may have little effect under these conditions,
thereby altering therapeutic response.

7) For drugs eliminated by first-order kinetics, half life is constant regardless of
concentration. With zero-order kinetics the term becomes meaningless, and one refers

Pharmacokinetic measurements of absorption, half-life, and metabolism are often done.
Phase 1 studies are usually performed in research centers by specially trained clinical
pharmacologists.
Start with very low dose. If there are only minor side effects, the next few participants might

though the ratio of fetal:maternal blood concentrations usually are not unity.

Pregnancy – transplacental movement of drugs
Factors that affect movement of drug from maternal into fetal circulation.
 Lipophilicity. Highly lipophilic drugs more easily cross placental cell membranes
(endothelial, placental) to enter into the fetal circulation.
 Protein binding. Highly protein-bound drugs have a lower free fraction that is available to
diffuse into the fetal circulation. However, if levels are maintained for long enough periods
of time (e.g., chronic dosing and always maintaining a therapeutic level on the maternal
side), the drug may eventually cross in significant amounts.
 Molecular weight. In general, drugs must be less than 400 to 500 Daltons to cross well, and
almost always less than 1000 Daltons to cross significantly into the fetal circulation.
 Drug pKa. Fetal pH is slightly lower than maternal pH. Therefore, some degree of ion
trapping can concentrate some drugs on the fetal side.
 The placenta contains some CYP450 drug-metabolizing enzymes, but it is not clear that
these have a major role in drug metabolism. Remember, however, that the placenta
inactivates prednisolone by converting it to prednisone, an inactive drug.

diffuse into the fetal circulation. However, if levels are maintained for long enough periods
of time (e.g., chronic dosing and always maintaining a therapeutic level on the maternal
side), the drug may eventually cross in significant amounts.
 Molecular weight. In general, drugs must be less than 400 to 500 Daltons to cross well, and
almost always less than 1000 Daltons to cross significantly into the fetal circulation.
 Drug pKa. Fetal pH is slightly lower than maternal pH. Therefore, some degree of ion
trapping can concentrate some drugs on the fetal side.
 The placenta contains some CYP450 drug-metabolizing enzymes, but it is not clear that
these have a major role in drug metabolism. Remember, however, that the placenta
inactivates prednisolone by converting it to prednisone, an inactive drug.

Why is PV important
No drug is 100% safe and without side effects for all people. In the US, it has been
estimated that 1 out of every 3 drugs has safety issues after approval.
Goal is to minimize the risks related to drugs used:
 Unexpected adverse reactions
 Drug interactions

 Quality of life
 Long-term efficacy
 Cost assessment - compares a drug's net cost (the price of the drug less any cost

Why we need PV
Clinical trials have many limitations
Known as the 5 “too”s
1) Too few sample populations in pre-marketing phase (0.1% of AE’s may be detected).
2) Too simple – in clinical trial the drug was only really evaluated for proof of efficacy.
Once the drug has been approved, patients who take it may also be taking other
drugs (concomitant).
3) Too median an age – the elderly and children are often not included in a clinical
trials. After approval, drug may be used in to treat children and the elderly.
4) Too narrow – administration, timing of drugs, monitoring etc are done by
professionals
5) Too brief – drugs used for many years, unlike the time used for clinical trials.

Historical background
Between 1934 – 1960 there was a vast increase in drug development
USA – Diethylene glycol (DEG) was used to solubilize sulfanilamide. Led to the deaths of
107 people.
Sulfanilamide, a drug used to treat streptococcal infections, had been shown to have
dramatic curative effects and had been used safely for some time in tablet and powder
form.
In June 1937, it was found that sulfanilamide would dissolve in diethylene glycol. The
company control lab tested the mixture for flavor, appearance, and fragrance and found it
satisfactory. Immediately, the company compounded a quantity of the elixir and sent
shipments-- 633 of them--all over the country.
The drug and the deaths led to the passage of the 1938 Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act,
which increased FDA's authority to regulate drugs.
